International Cheese Federation: Education Articles and Resources
This archive page from the International Cheese Federation features a collection of educational articles for cheesemakers. Topics covered include milk quality and herd health management, federal labeling requirements for dairy products, allergen control, Listeria prevention strategies for small creameries, adjustments to cheesemaking processes for seasonal milk variations, and insights into profitability for cheesemakers.

Reading your herd through the flush 

 

Spring flush changes what’s coming out of the bulk tank week to week. Our Milk Quality & Herd Health course exists for exactly that moving target.

What your label actually has to say 

 

The federal regulator closed a comment period this year on how dairy names get used on packaging. It’s a good moment for members to check their own labels, not just watch the debate.

Allergen controls, and the deadline that’s closer than it looks 

 

Small facilities have until September to meet federal preventive-controls allergen requirements. Our Allergen Management course starts March 29 — here’s what it actually covers.

What the herd decides before you do 

 

Milk composition shifts with the season, the feed, and the cow, long before it reaches your vat. Our Milk Quality & Herd Health course starts there instead of the recipe.

Listeria and the small cave: what environmental monitoring actually looks like 

 

Environmental monitoring sounds like a big-plant word, but it scales down fine. A look at what our Listeria Control course actually asks small creameries to do. 


Continue Reading

Winter milk, calcium balance, and the make sheet 

 

When dairy herds transition to winter rations, shifts in fat-to-protein ratios and soluble calcium can destabilize curd formation. Here is how craft creameries adjust make sheets and vat timing for cold-weather milk. 


Continue Reading

More revenue isn’t the same thing as more margin 

 

A new industry survey finds bigger cheesemakers often run thinner margins than small ones, a reminder that growth and profitability are separate problems.
